content.text: Route-plan's outgoing POST fails with 503 after 0.4–1.8 s, with no callee server span, and route-plan then returns 500, which travel-plan retries. To see which callee those 503s go to, I'll check how many route-plan client calls have a matching server span, split by status.

input.query: SELECT p, c.attr_http_response_status_code st, (s.span_id IS NOT NULL) has_child, count(*) n, round(avg(c.duration)/1e6,1) c_ms, round(avg(s.duration)/1e6,1) s_ms FROM (SELECT 'n' p,* FROM normal_traces UNION ALL SELECT 'a',* FROM abnormal_traces) c LEFT JOIN (SELECT trace_id, parent_span_id, span_id, duration FROM normal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Server' UNION ALL SELECT trace_id, parent_span_id, span_id, duration FROM abnormal_traces WHERE attr_span_kind='Server') s ON s.parent_span_id=c.span_id AND s.trace_id=c.trace_id WHERE c.service_name='ts-route-plan-service' AND c.attr_span_kind='Client' GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY 1,2,3

content.text: All 44 route-plan 503s lack a callee span, while every 200 has one, so the requests never reached the callee. To separate a network fault from an HTTP-layer fault on that edge, I'll check the drop and TCP-flag counters between route-plan and travel-service.
